paragraphs: A detailed 3D shape is not enough to simulate how an object deforms. A simulator also needs material properties throughout its volume, including stiffness, Poisson’s ratio, and density. AdaVoMP predicts these spatially varying properties for input 3D objects, turning geometric assets into objects that can participate in physical simulations.

The central design is a sparse, adaptive voxel structure that represents both the shape and its material field. Instead of using the fixed voxel layout of the earlier VoMP method, a transformer encoder-decoder generates a structure tailored to each input shape. It constructs that structure autoregressively, allowing the representation to adapt to the object while supporting greater resolution and memory efficiency.

The authors report a resolution increase of 16³ times over prior work, alongside more accurate volumetric property estimates. Their experiments also show these improvements with less test-time computation than the previous methods considered. The practical outcome is the conversion of complex, high-resolution objects into simulation-ready assets that produce realistic deformable behavior.
icml-2026-adaptive-volumetric-mechanical.tldr: AdaVoMP uses adaptive sparse voxels to predict detailed material properties for 3D objects with improved accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Some learning procedures fit a model and then use its predictions to guide a second fit on the same dataset. This happens in active learning and data reweighting. Reusing examples creates statistical dependencies: the second training objective already reflects information learned from those examples, so ordinary analyses of a single training stage do not directly apply.

The paper develops a precise asymptotic description of the second model’s test error for linear models with a broad family of convex losses on Gaussian mixture data. Its setting lets the number of examples and the number of features grow proportionally. Within that regime, the theory explicitly accounts for both data reuse and losses that depend on the first model’s predictions.

Applied to pool-based active learning, the analysis removes earlier assumptions requiring oracle information or separate data splits. It reveals a tradeoff in distributing a labeling budget between stages. It also identifies double descent caused solely by which data are selected, showing that this error pattern can arise without changing model size or sample count.
icml-2026-asymptotic-theory-of-iterated-.tldr: A high-dimensional theory explains two-stage learning with reused data and reveals how active data selection alone can produce double descent.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning learns representations by bringing related examples together and separating unrelated ones. The paper identifies a conflict when scenes share common features, such as blue sky. The same feature can be encouraged to match across positive pairs and pushed apart across negative pairs, producing competing gradient signals that interfere with separating meaningful concepts.

BayesNCL addresses this conflict through probabilistic feature gates. These gates filter frequent features that are irrelevant to the task while retaining features that distinguish examples. The authors formulate the selection process as variational inference with a sparse Bernoulli prior, making selective feature use part of the learning objective. This changes which information contributes to similarity comparisons instead of treating every feature dimension equally.

On ImageNet-100, the authors report a 142.1% improvement in semantic consistency relative to state-of-the-art baselines, without sacrificing downstream task performance. The finding supports their proposed connection between conflicting contrastive signals and entangled representations. In the reported experiments, resolving that conflict makes the learned features more interpretable while preserving their usefulness.
icml-2026-bayesian-gated-non-negative-co.tldr: BayesNCL uses probabilistic feature selection to reduce conflicting contrastive signals and improve representation interpretability without hurting reported downstream performance.

paragraphs: Selection can shape data in two different ways. A survey may include only volunteers, creating a filtered subset of an existing population. Evolution instead produces successive generations through differences in reproductive fitness. The paper argues that these processes need distinct causal models because the latest generation reflects a history of selection rather than a single filtering event.

The authors call these processes static and evolutionary selection. They show that the graphical model commonly used for selection is valid in static settings but fails to characterize evolutionary data, where it can produce false causal discoveries. Their contribution is a model designed specifically to represent evolutionary selection and the mechanisms responsible for the observed population.

They also develop an identification procedure described as sound and complete for this modeling framework, using data from one or multiple environments or generations. Experiments support its ability to recover relevant evolutionary mechanisms. The central implication is that causal discovery must distinguish selection of existing individuals from the repeated production of new generations shaped by differential fitness.
icml-2026-causal-modeling-of-selection-i.tldr: The paper separates one-time filtering from evolutionary selection and develops a causal model and identification procedure for the latter.

paragraphs: Standard language-model training focuses on predicting the next token. ContextLM adds a prediction objective for representations that cover several tokens, giving the model a training signal about what comes next at a broader level. The intended benefit is better next-token prediction through learning to anticipate the next context.

The framework builds language modeling on context embeddings and adds this next-context objective to ordinary pretraining. It therefore learns multi-token prediction implicitly while remaining compatible with standard autoregressive evaluation. A model can still be assessed token by token using perplexity, so the broader training objective does not require abandoning the familiar evaluation setup.

Experiments use GPT-2 and Pythia backbones at scales up to 1.5 billion parameters and 300 billion training tokens. The authors report improved tradeoffs among predictive performance, parameter count, training data, and computation. ContextLM reaches baseline perplexity with 39% fewer parameters and improves downstream generalization at equal parameter counts. These results suggest that the level at which prediction is taught can affect training efficiency, alongside the amount of model capacity and data.
icml-2026-context-level-language-modelin.tldr: ContextLM improves language-model efficiency by adding prediction of multi-token context embeddings to standard pretraining.

paragraphs: An attention weight describes how strongly a transformer weights a token’s value vector, but it does not fully describe that token’s contribution to the resulting representation. Vector magnitude and direction also matter. A token receiving substantial attention can have a different influence depending on how its value aligns with the layer output.

The paper introduces Contribution Weights, a projection-based measure that combines attention weight, value magnitude, and directional alignment. Across the decoder-only models, tasks, and datasets studied, this measure identifies semantically important tokens more faithfully than attention-based metrics. The approach makes the geometry of the aggregated information an explicit part of interpreting information flow.

The metric also supports a new analysis of attention sinks, tokens that attract attention disproportionately. The authors find an active role in suppressing information, expressed through a convex relationship between sink rate and output norm. They further describe sinks as stabilizing representations by opposing semantic drift from low-confidence tokens. This changes the interpretation of sinks from passive attention destinations to functional components of representation control.
icml-2026-contribution-weights-a-geometr.tldr: Contribution Weights incorporate value-vector geometry to better measure token influence and reveal a stabilizing role for attention sinks.

paragraphs: Some prediction targets are whole distributions, networks, or positive-definite matrices rather than ordinary numerical vectors. Their geometry requires a notion of prediction that respects distances in the output space. DeSI addresses this problem while also tackling high-dimensional inputs, which can make regression difficult when many variables must be considered jointly.

The framework assumes that the conditional Fréchet mean depends on the inputs through a single index: a one-dimensional combination of the input variables. A deep neural network estimates the index direction, whose coefficients indicate the relative importance of inputs. Fréchet regression then operates along that index in the target metric space, preserving the geometry of the structured outputs.

This single-index assumption provides the dimensional reduction that makes the approach interpretable and mitigates the curse of dimensionality. The authors establish uniform approximation and convergence-rate guarantees. Simulations cover distributions, networks, and positive-definite matrices, and an application uses compositional mood data from New Jersey. The reported predictive results show how neural estimation can support a structured regression model whose input dependence remains interpretable.
icml-2026-deep-single-index-frechet-regr.tldr: DeSI combines neural estimation of an interpretable one-dimensional input index with regression for outputs in metric spaces.

paragraphs: A reasoning language model can judge which of two responses is better, but a single judgment can be noisy. Repeating the judgment provides more evidence, yet aggregation becomes tricky when a tie is a valid answer. The paper studies how to use additional inference computation to turn repeated thinking-and-rating samples into more reliable evaluations.

Its method collects independent samples for each item and models the counts of the three possible preferences using a Bradley–Terry-Davidson formulation. It considers both polarity, the margin between the alternatives among non-tie judgments, and decisiveness, the fraction of judgments that are not ties. Together, these distinguish a preference supported by decisive agreement from a similar-looking margin surrounded by uncertainty.

Across evaluation benchmarks, the proposed aggregation reduces mean absolute error and improves pairwise accuracy relative to standard aggregation baselines. Against human-consensus labels, it matches or exceeds individual human raters. The findings concern agreement with those evaluation targets: they show that modeling the distribution of repeated judgments can make extra inference computation more useful than simply counting votes.
icml-2026-distribution-calibrated-infere.tldr: Modeling both preference margins and tie frequency makes repeated language-model judgments more accurate on the reported evaluation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Automated advertising bids must account for long-term outcomes while respecting budget and cost constraints. Learning directly through online experimentation can be prohibitively risky, motivating policies trained from historical records. The paper identifies a problem with approaches that compress several effective bidding strategies into one averaged action, especially when traffic is sparse or unusual.

DRIVE separates proposing bids from choosing among them. Its Transformer-based framework models a distribution of actions, retrieves candidate bids from high-quality historical decisions, and then evaluates the candidates by value. At inference time, the system selects the most promising bid from those proposals. This gives candidate generation access to both learned patterns and concrete historical decisions.

Experiments on AuctionNet and additional offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks show consistent improvements in bidding performance. The authors also report that the approach works across multiple Transformer-based methods. The result supports treating bid selection as a comparison among plausible alternatives, with retrieval supplementing the model’s learned action distribution when purely parametric predictions may be unreliable.
icml-2026-drive-distributional-and-retri.tldr: DRIVE improves offline bidding by generating diverse and retrieved candidate bids, then selecting among them using value estimates.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems have gradients that cannot be computed directly. Examples include maximum marginal likelihood estimation and tuning generative models. Stochastic approximation handles such problems using estimated gradients, but obtaining each estimate can require an inner sampling procedure. Repeating that procedure throughout optimization can become a major computational expense, even when the resulting estimates remain biased.

The paper develops sequential Monte Carlo samplers for this setting. The approach replaces expensive inner sampling methods with SMC approximations, aiming to make the sampling work within optimization more efficient. Its proposed benefit is computational: the authors state that this substitution can deliver substantial gains when optimizing functions with intractable gradients.

The theoretical results establish convergence for the underlying recursions that the SMC samplers approximate. This distinction identifies what the stated guarantees cover. Experiments demonstrate the approach on reward-based tuning of energy-based models in several settings. Together, the theory and experiments present a route to reducing the cost of sampling-dependent optimization while connecting the practical approximation to an analyzed recursive procedure.
icml-2026-efficient-stochastic-optimisat.tldr: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations can reduce the expensive inner sampling needed to optimize objectives with intractable gradients.

paragraphs: Training a diffusion model on a smaller dataset requires more than choosing individually convincing examples. The selected data must also preserve the structure of the full distribution. The paper argues that synthetic condensed datasets can lack fidelity, while existing methods for selecting real examples can lose the distributional geometry needed by diffusion likelihood objectives.

The proposed method treats real-data selection as a distribution-alignment problem. It uses one-sided partial optimal transport to align a compact subset with the full dataset while permitting some mass in low-density regions to remain unmatched. This makes the selection objective sensitive to geometric structure. Additional feature-statistics and semantic-consistency regularization support fidelity beyond the transport alignment itself.

A two-stage discrete optimization procedure selects the subset according to this combined objective. Experiments span diffusion variants, subset sizes, image resolutions, and training rounds, with reported improvements in both generated-sample fidelity and distributional coverage. The findings support designing condensed datasets around the requirements of generative training, where preserving relationships across examples matters alongside the quality of individual selected images.
icml-2026-geometry-aware-dataset-condens.tldr: Geometry-aware subset selection uses partial optimal transport to preserve the data structure needed for effective diffusion-model training.

paragraphs: Teacher-provided soft labels contain useful information about class relationships, but storing them for many image crops is costly. Reducing the number of stored crops introduces another problem: an ambiguous local crop can receive supervision that drifts away from the image’s ground-truth meaning. The paper studies this local semantic drift and the persistent errors it can create.

HALD uses hard labels as intermediate corrective signals while retaining the fine-grained information in soft labels. The image-level label provides a semantic anchor that does not change with crop content. The authors analyze how drift arises under sparse soft-label supervision and show how combining hard and soft supervision restores alignment between visual content and intended semantics.

Experiments on dataset distillation and large-scale classification report consistent generalization gains. On ImageNet-1K, the method reaches 42.7% accuracy with a reported soft-label storage amount of 285M, a 100-fold reduction, and outperforms LPLD by a reported 9.0%. The result shows that appropriately integrated hard labels can improve the accuracy–storage tradeoff in the studied setting.
icml-2026-hard-labels-in-rethinking-the-.tldr: HALD uses hard labels to correct semantic drift from sparse crop-level soft supervision, improving reported accuracy while sharply reducing label storage.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery requires a model to recognize familiar classes and discover unfamiliar ones. The paper argues that clustering objectives alone leave an important obstacle unresolved: standard visual backbones produce entangled patch representations that make underlying concepts and spatial structures difficult to identify. CPF-GCD changes the representation supplied to the discovery process.

Its central hypothesis is that known and novel categories can be expressed through combinations and spatial arrangements of a finite set of reusable visual primitives. A module placed between the backbone and prediction head rewrites patch tokens as low-rank mixtures of these primitives. A spatial field records where the primitives occur, representing an image through both its constituent parts and their arrangement.

Under this organization, a novel category can appear as a new activation pattern over an existing primitive vocabulary. Experiments show consistent improvements when the module is added to diverse category-discovery baselines. These results support low-rank compositional structure as a useful inductive bias for the evaluated open-world recognition tasks, linking discovery performance to how the feature space is organized.
icml-2026-identifying-latent-concepts-an.tldr: CPF-GCD improves category discovery by representing images as spatial arrangements of reusable visual primitives.

paragraphs: Induction heads are transformer attention circuits associated with learning patterns from the current context. This paper asks what statistical estimators those circuits implement when transformers are trained on order-k Markov chains. It identifies two mechanisms that smooth predictions, connecting attention behavior to classical methods for estimating sequence probabilities from limited observations.

First, at finite attention-weight scale, the circuit combines exact context matches with partial matches. Their contributions receive exponential weights based on overlap, producing a data-dependent interpolation across context lengths analogous to Jelinek–Merccer smoothing. Second, a beginning-of-sequence token contributes additive pseudo-counts, reproducing a Dirichlet-style smoothing mechanism. Both mechanisms temper estimates that would otherwise rely too heavily on observed counts.

The authors construct a transformer that separates these mechanisms and find the predicted attention patterns in trained models. Where pseudo-count smoothing is optimal or shorter contexts provide useful structured evidence, trained transformers match or outperform classical count-based baselines. The findings characterize induction heads as learning regularized in-context estimators, with prediction behavior shaped by both matching strength and the treatment of sparse evidence.
icml-2026-induction-heads-interpolate-n-.tldr: On Markov-chain tasks, induction heads implement context interpolation and pseudo-count smoothing that regularize in-context predictions.

paragraphs: Rationale-extraction models make predictions through two linked steps: selecting a subset of input features and predicting from that subset. The selected features form an interpretable rationale. Learning which subset to choose is difficult when the selector receives guidance only through the final prediction, because it must search among many possible feature combinations.

REKD gives smaller or less capable student models additional guidance from a teacher rationale-extraction model. The student learns from both the teacher’s selected rationales and its predictions while continuing its own rationale-extraction optimization. This supplies supervision for the intermediate selection step as well as the final answer, addressing the challenge of learning useful feature selection from distant task feedback.

The method is agnostic to the neural backbone, allowing different underlying networks to participate in the select-predict architecture. Experiments use BERT and vision-transformer variants on IMDB reviews, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. The authors report significant predictive improvements for student rationale-extraction models, showing that transferring intermediate interpretable selections can help smaller models learn this structured prediction process.
icml-2026-learn-from-a-rationalist-disti.tldr: REKD improves smaller rationale-extraction models by teaching them both a stronger model’s feature selections and its predictions.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation gives a language model external documents to help answer questions accurately and use current information. Large amounts of retrieved text also make the input expensive to process. Compressing that text can help, but a rule for deciding what looks important may discard information that the generation task actually needs.

CORE-RAG trains its compressor using task performance as feedback. It first uses knowledge distillation to initialize a useful compression policy, then iteratively refines that policy according to how well the resulting context supports the task. This directly connects compression decisions to the quality of generated answers, addressing the mismatch between predefined compression heuristics and downstream performance.

At the reported 3% compression ratio, CORE improves average Exact Match by 3.3 points compared with providing full documents. The experiments therefore show that substantial compression can coexist with better answer accuracy in the evaluated settings. The result makes context compression a learned part of task optimization, with efficiency and predictive quality assessed together rather than treating shorter input as the sole objective.
icml-2026-less-is-more-elevating-rag-via.tldr: CORE-RAG learns context compression from task feedback, achieving higher reported answer accuracy than full documents at a 3% compression ratio.

paragraphs: Deploying a model can change the data it later encounters. For example, people may alter their features to influence its decisions. Performative learning studies this feedback, where fitting the current distribution is only part of the problem. This paper examines how regularization can help when the exact resulting distribution shift is unknown.

The analysis focuses on high-dimensional ridge regression. It finds that performative effects worsen test risk in the population setting, but the picture changes when the model has more features than training examples. In that over-parameterized regime, optimal regularization in the presence of performativity reduces variability in the estimated parameters, which can improve performance.

The authors show that the optimal regularization scales with the overall strength of the performative effect. This provides a way to choose regularization in anticipation of feedback, rather than considering only the currently observed data. Synthetic and real-world evaluations illustrate the finding. The contribution links distributional response and estimation variance within the studied ridge-regression setting, explaining why their interaction matters for regularization.
icml-2026-optimal-regularization-for-per.tldr: In high-dimensional ridge regression, regularization tuned to performative feedback can reduce estimation variance and improve over-parameterized performance.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from confirmed positive examples and examples whose labels are unknown. When confirmed positives are extremely scarce, the paper finds that uncertainty in the positive part of the risk estimate dominates. Its generalization bound contains two contributors: the complexity of the candidate predictors and a range-dependent concentration term.

The authors derive a sufficient labeled-positive sample threshold for achieving a target excess risk with high probability. This is a threshold supplied by their guarantee, rather than a claim that fewer examples can never work. Their analysis makes explicit how both bound components affect the threshold and motivates separate ways to reduce them.

ScalePU uses variance regularization to restrict the effective hypothesis space and lower its Rademacher complexity. It also uses geometric regularization to encourage compact positive clusters and tighten the effective range. Theory shows that these mechanisms lower the sufficient threshold through different parts of the bound. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets report significant gains under extreme label scarcity, connecting the proposed regularizers to the identified sources of estimator instability.
icml-2026-positive-unlabeled-learning-wi.tldr: ScalePU targets two sources of risk-estimation uncertainty to improve positive-unlabeled learning when labeled positives are extremely scarce.

paragraphs: A robot cannot always choose its next action from what it currently sees. It may need to remember how many times an action was repeated or where an object was before it became hidden. RoboMME addresses the evaluation of these abilities in vision-language-action models, where previous memory tests have been narrow and difficult to compare systematically.

The benchmark contains 16 manipulation tasks organized around temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. This taxonomy gives researchers a common structure for testing different history-dependent demands. The authors also build 14 memory-augmented variants of the π0.5 backbone, varying both how memory is represented and how it is integrated into the policy.

The study finds that the effectiveness of a memory representation depends strongly on the task. Different designs have distinct advantages and limitations across the benchmark, making task coverage central to interpreting performance. RoboMME contributes both a standardized evaluation setting and a controlled collection of model variants for investigating which memory choices help with particular kinds of robotic manipulation.
icml-2026-robomme-benchmarking-and-under.tldr: RoboMME benchmarks four kinds of robotic memory and finds that effective memory designs depend strongly on the task.

paragraphs: Single-cell datasets can contain hundreds of millions of cells, making it necessary to load training data from disk. Fully random access provides diverse minibatches but incurs substantial storage-access overhead. Reading examples sequentially is faster, yet the resulting sampling biases can harm model performance. scDataset addresses this tension between loading efficiency and training-data diversity.

The method is a PyTorch data loader that combines block sampling with batched fetching. This produces quasi-random sampling: access is organized for efficient input/output while retaining diversity within training minibatches. The loader works across multiple storage formats, and the authors provide theoretical bounds on minibatch diversity to characterize the statistical side of this design.

On the 100-million-cell Tahoe-100M dataset, scDataset delivers more than a hundredfold speedup over true random sampling while reading AnnData files directly. Across multiple classification tasks and model architectures, it matches the predictive performance achieved with true random sampling. These results show that carefully organizing disk access can substantially accelerate data loading without losing the training benefits of diverse minibatches in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-scdataset-scalable-data-loadin.tldr: scDataset combines block sampling and batched reads to accelerate single-cell data loading while matching random-sampling classification performance.

paragraphs: Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient, or SVRG, uses gradient corrections to accelerate training. This paper gives those corrections a Bayesian interpretation by connecting SVRG to posterior correction. The contribution provides a common derivation for an established optimization method and a Bayesian procedure, allowing the latter to guide the construction of new optimizers.

The authors show that SVRG is recovered when posterior correction operates over isotropic Gaussian posteriors. This specific posterior family therefore reproduces the familiar algorithm. Moving to more flexible exponential-family posteriors produces extensions of SVRG, making the choice of probability family a way to determine the form of the resulting training update.

Using Gaussian families, the paper derives two extensions: a Newton-like method with new Hessian corrections and an Adam-like method that scales to large problems. These examples demonstrate how the Bayesian connection generates concrete optimization procedures beyond the original gradient correction. The broader significance is methodological: posterior correction becomes a framework for deriving variance-reduced training algorithms and understanding their relationship to existing optimizer designs.
icml-2026-svrg-and-beyond-via-posterior-.tldr: A Bayesian posterior-correction view recovers SVRG and yields new Newton-like and Adam-like optimization methods.

paragraphs: TextMesh4D generates dynamic 3D meshes from text using pretrained diffusion guidance. Such assets could help address the cost of capturing and annotating dynamic 3D data. Direct mesh generation is challenging because diffusion guidance can be noisy and spatially inconsistent, while a mesh imposes structural constraints that make direct vertex deformation unstable.

The method addresses geometry and semantic consistency separately. For geometry, a Jacobian Deformation Field models changes at the level of faces rather than individual vertices. An integration formulation enforces integrability, bringing those local changes into a coherent surface. For semantics, a Local-Global Semantic Regularizer constrains local deformation plausibility and global shape consistency to preserve the object’s identity over time.

The authors describe TextMesh4D as the first zero-shot text-to-4D framework to generate dynamic meshes directly. Experiments report state-of-the-art temporal consistency, structural fidelity, and visual quality, with efficient operation on a single 24GB GPU. The contribution shows how deformation representation and semantic constraints can help reconcile diffusion-based generation with the requirements of temporally coherent mesh surfaces.
icml-2026-textmesh4d-zero-shot-text-to-4.tldr: TextMesh4D combines face-based deformation and semantic regularization to generate temporally coherent dynamic meshes from text.

paragraphs: Consumer AI adoption changes how people discuss and use these products, but those changes can be difficult to track systematically. This paper develops a framework for studying societal impacts through social-media data, together with a method for detecting emerging trends in real time. It applies the framework to a longitudinal analysis of r/ChatGPT.

Across the period studied, posts increasingly portray ChatGPT as an ordinary consumer product rather than an exceptional new technology. The retrospective analysis also finds that posts about mental-health support and emotional attachment rise steadily in frequency immediately after GPT-4o’s launch in May 2024. These are observed changes in subreddit discussion; the reported timing does not by itself establish that the launch caused them.

The authors show that their real-time monitoring method could detect increased emotional engagement by October 2024, months before OpenAI publicly acknowledged this impact. The study demonstrates how structured analysis of an online community can identify changing patterns of AI use and flag socially consequential developments earlier than later public recognition.
icml-2026-three-years-of-r-chatgpt-socie.tldr: An analysis of r/ChatGPT tracks AI’s normalization and shows how social-media monitoring can detect rising emotional engagement.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks approximate solutions to differential equations while enforcing physical equations and boundary and initial conditions. For time-dependent problems, standard architectures accept time as an input but keep the same network weights at every moment. The paper argues that this forces shared features to represent substantially different dynamics, which can reduce accuracy and destabilize training.

Time-Induced Neural Networks make the network weights a learned function of time. The effective representation of space can therefore evolve as the solution changes, while the model retains shared structure across time. This modifies the representation itself rather than relying entirely on a fixed network to express all temporal behavior through its inputs.

The resulting training formulation is a nonlinear least-squares problem, optimized with a Levenberg–Marquardt method. Across the time-dependent PDEs tested, the authors report up to fourfold improvement in relative L2 error and tenfold faster convergence compared with PINNs and strong baselines. These are reported maximum gains, supporting time-dependent parameterization as a useful approach for the evaluated problems.
icml-2026-tinns-time-induced-neural-netw.tldr: TINNs learn network weights as a function of time to improve the accuracy and convergence of neural PDE solvers.

paragraphs: Large language models trained with abundant resources may contain useful capabilities for smaller models operating in low-resource languages or specialized domains. Model merging offers a route to transfer, but many existing approaches require compatible architectures. That requirement makes it difficult to combine a large source model with a structurally different target.

This paper uses optimal transport to infer correspondences between neurons from their activations. Rather than assuming that units already line up across models, it estimates how their responses relate. The resulting transport plans then guide direct fusion in weight space. Only a small set of inputs is used to support this cross-architecture transfer process.

Experiments across low-resource languages and specialized domains show consistent improvements over the target models. The findings support activation alignment as a practical bridge between heterogeneous architectures, enabling the source model’s information to influence the target’s weights. The contribution extends the applicability of merging to a setting where architectural differences otherwise prevent direct transfer through conventional compatibility-dependent methods.
icml-2026-transport-and-merge-cross-arch.tldr: Optimal-transport alignment enables direct weight merging between differently structured language models to improve low-resource targets.
